name: cap-errors
description: One typed, machine-readable failure object for every boundary: RFC 9457 problem details and a closed registry of problem types. Load when deciding what a failure returns, adding a failure mode or type URI, when a component defines its own error object, when a caller must parse prose, or when a status code alone drives retry.

purpose.text: Give every failure in the platform one typed, machine-readable shape so no caller ever parses prose, by adopting the standard named for this capability whole instead of designing an error object of our own.
purpose.quote: Typed and machine-readable. Never parsed from prose

standards.version_note: RFC 9457 (a search-only research record dates it July 2023 and says it obsoletes RFC 7807; the specification was not fetched from this environment)

operations.name: raise (operation name is ours; the object it constructs is the standard's)
operations.input: a registered type suffix, a detail string written for the caller, and the extension members that type declares
operations.output: a Problem value carrying type, title, status, detail and those extensions; construction fails when the suffix has no row in the closed registry
operations.quote: type (URI identifying the error category), title (short human-readable summary), status (HTTP status code), detail (specific explanation)

operations.name: render (operation name is ours; the wire object is the standard's)
operations.input: a Problem value and the transport it leaves through
operations.output: the problem-details JSON object plus the media type application/problem+json; the same object serialises for a stdio, message or HTTP seam, so the shape does not oblige a transport

operations.name: classify (proposed; adapter-unavailable and its counter are this platform's own mechanism, not the standard's)
operations.input: any failure raised beneath a capability adapter, including one the adapter did not type
operations.output: a registered Problem, or adapter-unavailable carrying the untyped payload in detail and incrementing the adapter's untyped counter. Research query: has any adapter in this repo been run through a suite that counts its untyped-failure rate, which would turn this from a designed mechanism into a measured one?

operations.name: retry_advice (proposed; the members are the standard's, the read-never-infer rule is ours)
operations.output: the explicit retryable boolean and the optional retry_after_s, read from the members and never inferred from the status code

operations.name: chain (proposed operation; the causes array is ours, not part of the base schema)
operations.input: an outer Problem and the inner Problem that caused it
operations.output: the outer Problem with the inner appended to causes, innermost last, so a delegated failure keeps its origin instead of being flattened into a sentence. Research query: does any recorded RFC 9457 extension example chain problems via a causes-style array, or is nesting causes this platform's own addition to the base schema?

shapes.name: Problem (from docs/decomposition.md section 2.1.6; the required members are the standard's, retryable/correlation_id/causes are this platform's extensions; the full schema and the closed type registry are in references/problem-registry.md)

type.description: urn:agentic:problem:<suffix>. The suffix must have a row in the closed registry; an unregistered value is a conformance failure.

detail.description: Written so the caller can act. Never a stack trace, and never the criterion a result is judged against.

retryable.description: Explicit. The platform profile emits it on every problem even though the standard keeps its members optional.

shapes.quote: type (URI identifying the error category), title (short human-readable summary), status (HTTP status code), detail (specific explanation), and instance (URI identifying the specific request)

shapes.name: Worked example 2 (proposed): an agent's next step would cross the ceiling [caller's view, folded from cap-errors-use]

schema.title: A step would cross the budget ceiling
schema.description: Exit code 2, refused before the step ran, so the ledger shows no dispatch for it.

examples.title: A step would cross the budget ceiling

invariants.text: Every failure the platform returns is typed and machine-readable; a caller branches on the type member and never on the words in the message.
invariants.quote: Typed and machine-readable. Never parsed from prose

invariants.text: The governing standard is RFC 9457 problem details and the recorded instruction for this capability is to adopt the RFC directly, so there is no bespoke error object to design here. agentic-stack states design rule 2 (F-b1-03); this row is only its application to Errors.
invariants.quote: — adopt the RFC directly

invariants.text: The starting point is nothing rather than something: what runs today records Typed errors as Absent, so this capability is adopted, not migrated.
invariants.quote: Typed errors | Absent

invariants.text: Every failure body of every seam and every adapter carries the media type application/problem+json, whatever transport it leaves through: a Problem Details response uses that content type and includes the fields type, title, status, detail and instance, extensible with application-specific fields. Docs/decomposition.md section 2.1.6 fixes this for the platform (proposed).
invariants.quote: A Problem Details response uses the application/problem+json content type and includes fields: type (URI identifying the error category), title (short human-readable summary), status (HTTP status code), detail (specific explanation), and instance (URI identifying the specific request).

invariants.text: The type member must resolve to a row in the closed registry in docs/decomposition.md section 2.1.6: the governing standard itself keeps an IANA registry for problem type URIs and requires registration before reuse. An unregistered type URI is a conformance failure on this platform (proposed, stricter than the standard's own Specification-Required bar), and extending the set means adding a row there before any code emits it. Proposed: a skill may state an unregistered suffix only while it is marked proposed and pending registration with a registered fallback named; tools/validate_skills.py warns per suffix when that marker is missing.
invariants.quote: RFC 9457 introduces an IANA registry for hosting common problem type URIs. The registry promotes reuse of widely used problem types and requires Specification Required registration for new entries.

invariants.text: retryable is a member, never an inference from the status code, so a 503 that must not be retried says so. The base schema keeps all standard members optional and allows problem-specific extensions, which is why the platform profile (proposed) is what requires retryable on emission rather than the standard.
invariants.quote: The base schema keeps all standard members optional and allows problem-specific extensions.

invariants.text: Proposed: a failure that cannot be typed is itself a conformance failure of the adapter that raised it. It is returned as adapter-unavailable with the untyped payload in detail and it is counted; an adapter whose untyped count is non-zero is not conformant, however green its own tests are. Research query: has any adapter in this repo actually been run through a suite that counts its untyped-failure rate, or is 'however green its own tests are' an assertion with no measured adapter behind it yet?

Consequence of design rule 6, which agentic-stack states under F-b1-07: an agent sees its outcome, never the criterion it is judged against. A problem body is caller-visible (proposed), so the criterion a result is judged against must never appear in detail, in causes, or in any extension member.
invariants.quote: the criterion it is judged against.

invariants.text: A human, an event, a schedule and an external system or agent get the same object. All four entry kinds enter through the same shape, and the failure half is not specialised per entry, so one handler covers every way work arrived.
invariants.quote: All four enter through the same shape.

invariants.text: Enhancing one aspect leaves the rest untouched: adding a registry row, changing a title, or swapping which adapter produces the body changes nothing in a caller that reads type and retryable, because those are the only members it was ever asked to branch on.
invariants.quote: Composability allows enhancing particular aspects of any element without touching the rest.

not_exposed.text: Stack traces, internal hostnames, credentials and adapter identities stay out of the problem body: products belong in the adapter column only. agentic-stack states that rule (F-part-c-09); the consequence here (proposed) is that a caller cannot tell which implementation failed from the failure it receives.
not_exposed.quote: Products belong in the adapter column only.

not_exposed.text: The criterion the Judge grades against is not exposed through the failure path, which is the one path most likely to leak it while explaining why something did not pass: an agent sees its outcome, never the criterion it is judged against (proposed application of design rule 6).
not_exposed.quote: the criterion it is judged against.

not_exposed.text: Proposed: the transport is not part of the contract. The shape and its media type are adopted; the HTTP binding is not required for this object to be the failure shape of a stdio or message-based seam. Research query: has this shape actually been round-tripped over a non-HTTP transport (stdio or a message queue) to confirm the media type alone travels cleanly, or is transport-independence argued rather than run?

instructions.action: Take the member set and the media type of the standard as given and design nothing: the recorded instruction for this capability is to adopt the RFC directly.
instructions.why: The swap-candidate column for Errors is not a list of alternatives; it is the instruction. An original error object here would be original design where a published decision already exists.
instructions.quote: — adopt the RFC directly

instructions.action: Define the failure object as the five standard members and treat everything else as an extension member: type identifying the error category, title, status, detail, instance identifying the specific request.
instructions.why: A response uses the application/problem+json content type and includes fields: type (URI identifying the error category), title (short human-readable summary), status (HTTP status code), detail (specific explanation), and instance (URI identifying the specific request).
instructions.quote: uses the application/problem+json content type and includes fields: type (URI identifying the error category), title (short human-readable summary), status (HTTP status code), detail (specific explanation), and instance (URI identifying the specific request)

instructions.action: Proposed: register the platform's own problem-type namespace as urn:agentic:problem:<suffix> and keep it a closed registry, each row fixing the suffix, the status, whether it is retryable and when it is raised. Add a row to docs/decomposition.md section 2.1.6 before any code emits a new suffix. When a failure mode has no row in that registry, apply 1-3-1 rather than minting a suffix at the call site: state the problem, list the three best registry changes, follow the recommendation, and record it as an open question with the row you would add. Until that row lands, the skill that needs the type marks the suffix proposed and pending registration in the same sentence that states it and names the registered type an implementation returns meanwhile, carrying the proposed suffix in detail, so no caller branches on a URI no conformant implementation may emit. Emit retryable on every problem, and pair it with retry_after_s where the wait is knowable, instead of leaving a caller to read the status code.
instructions.why: From docs/decomposition.md section 2.1.6 (proposed). The standard's own registry promotes reuse of widely used problem types and requires Specification Required registration for new entries, and a namespace that anyone may extend at the call site is not a registry. The same act governs the missing row: when a problem comes up, use 1-3-1: define the problem, identify the three best possible solutions that align to the goal, and follow the recommendation. Best practice for this standard is to include Retry-After on 429 and 503 responses. What this adds (proposed, platform profile): a boolean alone cannot carry the rate-limited case; the status code alone cannot distinguish a 503 that will clear from one that will not.
instructions.quote: The registry promotes reuse of widely used problem types and requires Specification Required registration for new entries.

instructions.action: Emit retryable on every problem, and pair it with retry_after_s where the wait is knowable, instead of leaving a caller to read the status code.
instructions.why: Best practice for this standard is to include Retry-After on 429 and 503 responses. What this adds (proposed, platform profile): a boolean alone cannot carry the rate-limited case; the status code alone cannot distinguish a 503 that will clear from one that will not.
instructions.quote: Include Retry-After on 429 and 503 responses

instructions.action: Return all validation errors at once with field-level detail, in one problem, rather than one problem per offending field.
instructions.why: Return all validation errors at once with field-level detail; a caller that has to resubmit once per field learns the shape of its own mistake one round trip at a time.
instructions.quote: return all validation errors at once with field-level detail

instructions.action: Treat an untyped failure as a defect of the adapter that raised it. Map it to adapter-unavailable, carry the untyped payload in detail, count it, and judge an implementation conformant only when that count is zero. Research query: see the untyped-failure-count research query on the sibling invariant row above.
instructions.why: Proposed, from docs/decomposition.md section 2.1.6. Without the counter, the adapters that never learned to type their failures are exactly the ones a conformance run cannot see, because they answer with something rather than nothing.

instructions.action: Proposed: keep the object bound to its media type and not to HTTP, so a stdio, message or in-process seam returns the identical body and a caller writes one branch for all of them. Research query: see the transport-independence research query on the sibling not_exposed row above.
instructions.why: Proposed, from docs/decomposition.md section 1. The standard defines a media type and a member set; nothing forces the transport to be HTTP for the shape to be adopted, and binding it to one transport would make the failure path the only part of a seam that cannot be swapped.

instructions.action: Before declaring an implementation done, grep every problem body it can emit for the text of the criterion the result is judged against, and treat a hit as a rule-6 breach rather than a wording problem.
instructions.why: agentic-stack states design rule 6 under F-b1-07: an agent sees its outcome, never the criterion it is judged against. The consequence specific to this capability (proposed) is that the failure path is the path most tempted to explain why something did not pass.
instructions.quote: the criterion it is judged against.

instructions.action: Branch on the type member and nothing else. Do not match on title, detail, exit codes or log lines.
instructions.why: Errors are typed and machine-readable, never parsed from prose; title and detail are written for people and may be reworded without notice.
instructions.quote: Typed and machine-readable. Never parsed from prose

best_practices.text: Write detail for the person who has to fix it: the detail field should help developers fix the problem without contacting support. A detail that only names the failure repeats the type member.
best_practices.quote: The detail field should help developers fix the problem without contacting support.

best_practices.text: Prefer a widely used registered problem type to a locally minted one: the standard's registry promotes reuse of widely used problem types and requires Specification Required registration for new entries, so a private suffix is a cost paid by every client that has to learn it.
best_practices.quote: The registry promotes reuse of widely used problem types and requires Specification Required registration for new entries.

best_practices.text: The reason to adopt rather than invent is stated by the standard itself: it exists to carry machine-readable details of errors in HTTP response content, avoiding the need to define new error response formats. Every bespoke error object is one more format a client must learn.
best_practices.quote: to carry machine-readable details of errors in HTTP response content

best_practices.text: Copy the correlation identifier onto the problem body, not only into the log line: structured logs should be in JSON format and include correlation IDs for error tracking, and agentic-stack states the correlation finding (F-a7-02: correlation must ride on an explicit resource attribute set at dispatch). What this adds (proposed): the failure a caller holds is often the only artifact that survives the boundary.
best_practices.quote: structured logs should be in JSON format and include correlation IDs for error tracking

best_practices.text: Cite the current RFC, not the one a library's documentation names: RFC 7807 has been succeeded by RFC 9457, so a dependency that still speaks of 7807 is describing an older member set than the one this contract adopts.
best_practices.quote: RFC 7807 has been succeeded by RFC 9457

open_questions.question: Do problem details need a structured retry policy or a boolean? (docs/decomposition.md section 5 question 9)
open_questions.evidence: Across the run history, count how many distinct failure types actually differ in the retry behaviour a caller should adopt. If the answer is two or three, a policy object is over-modelled.
open_questions.default: The boolean plus retry_after_s, as in this skill's Problem shape. It is one optional member and it covers the rate-limited case that a boolean alone cannot.

open_questions.question: Whose spelling of the type suffixes is normative? The manifest's fold-in names budget-exceeded, cancelled, timeout, schema-invalid and partial-result, while the closed registry in docs/decomposition.md section 2.1.6 spells the same concerns budget-exhausted, cancel-timeout, deadline-exceeded and document-invalid, and has no partial-result row at all.
open_questions.evidence: An edit to docs/decomposition.md section 2.1.6 that renames or adds the rows, which is the only sanctioned way to change a closed registry. Until that edit exists, the two lists are the same set of concerns under different names.
open_questions.default: 1-3-1 as build-evidence states it (T-t5-02, folded from build-definition-of-done), applied and recorded on 2026-09-03. Options considered: (a) rename the registry to the manifest's words; (b) keep the registry's words and read the manifest's list as the same concerns; (c) carry both as aliases. Recommendation and default: (b). The registry is closed and renaming it without the row edit is the move the note itself forbids, aliases would let two spellings of one type reach clients, and partial-result is not a failure at all because a partial result returns through the result shape rather than through a problem body.
open_questions.quote: define the problem, identify the three best possible solutions that align to the goal, and follow the recommendation

cap-errors-implement.name: cap-errors-implement
cap-errors-implement.description: How to build the Errors capability on this stack: the first adapter, a second one with a different execution model, what to do when there is nothing to migrate from, how the budget, policy, identity, idempotency and correlation guarantees land in a failure body, and a definition of done with the breakage that makes it fail. Load it when you are writing or reviewing the code that produces a failure, when wiring a capability adapter's failure path, when adding an edge component that answers on behalf of a service, when a cross-cutting concern needs somewhere to report a refusal, or when a conformance run reports untyped failures and you have to find which adapter produced them.

purpose.text: Turn the contract in cap-errors into something that runs here: two adapters behind one failure shape, every untyped failure path converted, and every cross-cutting refusal landing on a registered problem type rather than in a log line.
purpose.quote: Typed and machine-readable. Never parsed from prose

shapes.name: ErrorsConformanceReport (proposed shape; the counters that the definition of done below asserts on)

adapters_run.description: Distinct adapters exercised. Fewer than two means the swap was not tested.

adapter.description: Adapter entity id, so a failure names one implementation and not the capability.

untyped.description: Failures the adapter could not type. Non-zero means this adapter is not conformant.

invariants.text: Proposed: the two adapters differ on processes_required_for_progress, in the sense build-adapter-pair defines. The first raises and renders the problem inside the failing process; the second is a separate process on the response path that never enters the service. A pair that agrees on that axis proves nothing and is rejected. Research query: is there a recorded conformance run distinguishing the two adapters' process counts on this axis, which would turn this claim from an assertion into a measured finding?

Proposed: the swap is configuration. No caller, and no code in the core, selects between the adapters or branches on which one answered; agentic-stack states design rule 1 (F-b1-02) and this is its consequence for the failure path.
invariants.quote: The core imports interfaces, never implementations.

invariants.text: Proposed: there is nothing to migrate. cap-errors carries the row recording typed errors as Absent (F-a6-06), so the work is conversion of untyped failure paths rather than translation of an existing error object, and the count of converted paths is the progress measure.
invariants.quote: Typed errors | Absent

invariants.text: A budget refusal lands on the budget-exhausted row because exceeding a ceiling terminates the unit, not the platform: the problem body is what tells the caller which of the two happened.
invariants.quote: Every unit of work carries a ceiling. Exceeding it terminates the unit, not the platform

invariants.text: A policy refusal lands on the policy-denied row carrying rule_id, and it is emitted before any spend, because refusal is deterministic and happens before execution, not after spend.
invariants.quote: Refusal is deterministic and happens before execution, not after spend

invariants.text: A replayed externally-triggered action with the same key and a different body lands on the idempotency-conflict row, because every externally-triggered action is safe to replay and a conflict is the one case where that promise cannot be kept silently.
invariants.quote: Every externally-triggered action is safe to replay

invariants.text: Proposed: none of these wirings is optional and none is requested by the caller. agentic-stack states the no-opt-out rule (F-b1-08, F-b4-01); what this adds is that the failure body is where a caller would first notice an opt-out, because a declined guarantee has no registered type to report under.
invariants.quote: The platform applies each; a caller cannot decline them

invariants.text: Proposed: every claim in this skill is claimed until the conformance report exists, recorded the way build-evidence-record requires. No adapter here has been run, so nothing about their behaviour may be labelled measured.

instructions.action: Build the first adapter in-process: one library that owns the closed registry, constructs a Problem only from a registered suffix, and refuses construction otherwise. Do not let handlers assemble the object field by field.
instructions.why: Proposed. If the registry is data the library enforces rather than a table in a document, an unregistered type cannot reach a client at all, which turns the registry invariant in cap-errors into a compile- or construct-time failure instead of a conformance-run finding. Research query: is there a recorded conformance run in this repository proving that an unregistered problem type actually fails to construct, rather than this being an asserted design intention?

instructions.action: Enumerate every failure path in what runs, map each to a registry row, and convert them one at a time. Where the failure has no row, route it through classify to adapter-unavailable and increment the untyped counter rather than inventing a suffix.
instructions.why: cap-errors carries the row recording typed errors as Absent (F-a6-06, E-not-running-typed-errors), so this is conversion from nothing rather than migration from an existing shape; the counter is what stops an unconverted path from looking finished.
instructions.quote: Typed errors | Absent

instructions.action: Build the second adapter as a filter at the edge that maps an upstream failure into the problem-details body without the service being touched, and record its execution-model difference against the first as build-adapter-pair requires.
instructions.why: The second exists to prove the first is not load-bearing: an in-process library and an edge filter disagree about how many processes must run for a failure to be produced and about how much context is available at the point of production, which is what makes the pair evidence rather than a spare.
instructions.quote: the second exists to prove the first is not load-bearing

instructions.action: Give the second adapter the failing case honestly: it can only see the wire response, so it cannot populate rule_id, causes or the raise-site detail unless the service already emitted them. Declare that gap in the pair's record instead of widening the interface to close it.
instructions.why: build-adapter-pair (F-meta-04) is explicit that a boundary needing a core change to complete a swap is drawn wrong; widening the contract so both adapters can satisfy every member is that failure applied to the failure path, so the honest alternative is a declared gap that the conformance suite asserts on.
instructions.quote: If Part B cannot swap an implementation without touching the core, the boundary is drawn wrong

instructions.action: Wire the cross-cutting refusals to their rows: budget to budget-exhausted with the spend that would have crossed the ceiling, policy to policy-denied carrying rule_id and emitted before any spend, identity to identity-untrusted, idempotency to idempotency-conflict.
instructions.why: Each concern already has a contract; the failure body is where a caller observes it. Refusal is deterministic and happens before execution, not after spend, so a policy problem emitted after a metered call is the wrong object at the wrong time.
instructions.quote: Refusal is deterministic and happens before execution, not after spend

instructions.action: Proposed: copy the explicit correlation attribute set at dispatch onto every problem body, and assert in the conformance suite that it survives both adapters.
instructions.why: Proposed wiring. agentic-stack states the correlation finding (F-a7-02); the consequence here is that the edge-filter adapter mints its response outside the failing process, so a body that inherits nothing is exactly the case that finding predicts.
instructions.quote: Correlation must ride on an explicit resource attribute set at dispatch.

instructions.action: Write one conformance suite against the capability and parameterise it over adapters, selecting the adapter by configuration with no code edit between runs, and emit the report shape defined above.
instructions.why: Per design rule 1 as agentic-stack and build-adapter-pair state it (F-b1-02), the core imports interfaces, never implementations, so the suite must import the capability and never an adapter type; a per-adapter branch inside the suite would test two things and prove neither swappable.
instructions.quote: The core imports interfaces, never implementations

instructions.action: Verify at runtime which adapter actually answered, rather than trusting the configuration that selected it, by asserting the report's adapter field against a marker the running adapter emits.
instructions.why: agentic-stack already states the configuration finding (F-a7-04): values written to the documented place validated, reviewed correctly, and had no runtime effect. What this step adds, as this skill's own consequence and proposed: assert the report's adapter field against a marker the running adapter emits rather than against the binding record, because a swap job that never left the first adapter reports two green runs of the same code.
instructions.quote: Values written to YAML validated, reviewed correctly, and had no runtime effect

instructions.action: Apply build-definition-of-done: run the definition of done below and then its deliberate breakage, and record both outputs as an evidence record the way build-evidence-record fixes, before calling this facet done; proposed pointer, see those skills.
instructions.why: build-definition-of-done owns criterion plus deliberate breakage plus both recorded outputs, and build-evidence-record owns what the record names, so this row points at them instead of restating the sentence six sibling -implement skills had copied (consolidation part B, kb/ceremonies/implement-clusters.json).
instructions.quote: A criterion nothing can fail is not a criterion.

xc-typed-errors.name: xc-typed-errors
xc-typed-errors.description: The cross-cutting guarantee that no failure anywhere in this platform is discovered by matching strings: every failure-producing site returns one typed problem object drawn from one shared closed registry, whichever way the caller entered, and no caller, adapter or fast path can decline it. Load it when a component is about to inspect a message, a log line or a response body to work out what went wrong, when a retry heuristic keys on a substring such as rate limit or timed out, when a new failure-producing site or a new way into the system is added, when a refusal has a different shape depending on whether a person, another system or a timer triggered the work, when an implementation reports an untyped failure and someone proposes recording it as a known gap, and when auditing that the ban on string matching is enforced rather than agreed.

purpose.text: Make it a checked property of the whole tree that failure information is never extracted by matching a string: every codepath that can fail returns the typed object cap-errors defines, every driving adapter reads the same closed type registry, and the count of sites that still read prose is asserted to zero rather than tracked.

standards.version_note: cap-errors owns the standards row for this capability and records the version a search-only record names; no specification was fetched from this environment, and this layer places the object rather than defining it

operations.name: type_or_count (proposed; the platform's call at every boundary, not a caller's)
operations.input: any failure crossing any boundary of the platform, including one the code beneath it raised as a message, an exception or a non-2xx body
operations.output: a problem object whose type has a row in the closed registry, or the registered adapter-unavailable type carrying the untyped payload in detail and incrementing that boundary's untyped counter; there is no third outcome and no pass-through

operations.name: branch (proposed; what a caller is given instead of a message)
operations.output: the type member and the declared extension members the registry row names for that type; the operation exposes no message string as a branch key, so a caller that wanted to match on prose has nothing to match against

operations.name: resolve_type (proposed; one registry behind every way in)
operations.input: a failure condition raised anywhere beneath any driving adapter, plus the entry kind the work arrived through
operations.output: the same registry row whichever entry kind was supplied; the entry kind is recorded on the problem and is never an input to the type decision, so one refusal cannot become two types

operations.name: audit_string_matching (proposed)
operations.input: the whole source tree and the single path that holds the problem-details parser
operations.output: the count of sites outside that path that extract failure information by matching a string, plus the untyped-failure count per boundary; zero is the only conformant value for both, counted over the population and never sampled

shapes.name: TypedErrorAudit (proposed): the machine-readable report the definition of done asserts on; the per-boundary mapping and the audit's blind spots are in references/xc-typed-errors-typed-errors-audit.md

parser_path.description: The one path the string-match audit excludes, because parsing prose into a type is that path's job and nowhere else's.

string_match_sites.description: Sites outside parser_path that read failure information out of a string. Zero is the only conformant value.

failures_checked.description: Non-zero by construction: an audit that observed no failure cannot report that every failure was typed.

shared_refusal_type.description: The type returned for one refusal condition raised under every entry kind. One value, or the guarantee has already failed.

shapes.name: FailureAtEveryEntry (worked instances: what comes back to a human, an event, a schedule, and an external system or agent, which are T6.2's four doors; each is an actual problem object with a registered type, and the caller supplies nothing to get it)

problem.description: The failure object cap-errors defines. Only the members a caller branches on are shown here; the full schema and the closed registry belong to that skill.

problem.title: A policy rule refused this dispatch
problem.detail: rule egress.external-http refused the step; no metered call was made

problem.title: A metered call would cross the ceiling
problem.detail: ceiling reached at step 4; the unit was terminated and the run was not

problem.title: Envelope failed schema validation
problem.detail: intent.workflow_ref is required and was absent

problem.title: A capability adapter answered without a type
problem.detail: the untyped payload is carried here and the boundary's untyped counter was incremented

shapes.quote: Four entries cover nearly every situation: a human, an event, a schedule (time), and an external system or agent.

invariants.text: cap-errors owns the failure object, its members and the closed type registry (F-b4-07). What this layer adds is the placement and the count: the rule binds every failure-producing site in the tree, not only the sites a client library happens to cover, and it is asserted as a number rather than agreed as a convention.
invariants.quote: Never parsed from prose

invariants.text: Every codepath that can fail must produce a typed, machine-readable error with consistent schema, and the scope is both kinds of failure at once: structural failures such as network, authentication and resource exhaustion, and behavioural failures such as a policy refusal, a validation failure or a state conflict.
invariants.quote: Every codepath that can fail must produce a typed, machine-readable error with consistent schema.

invariants.text: One shared type registry sits behind every driving adapter, so a policy refusal, a budget termination and a validation failure carry the same type whichever way the work entered. The driving side is the several adapters that initiate actions into one core, and a registry held per adapter would give one refusal as many names as there are ways in.
invariants.quote: The driving (primary) side consists of actors and adapters that initiate actions into the application core

invariants.text: The guarantee holds across the whole structure and not per entry point: state, telemetry, and every cross-cutting concern are managed across the entire structure, so an audit that exercised one way in has proved the property for that one and asserted it for the rest.
invariants.quote: State, telemetry, and every cross-cutting concern are managed across the entire structure

invariants.text: A caller cannot decline it. agentic-stack states design rule 7 (F-b1-08), that the four cross-cutting guarantees are applied by the platform rather than requested; the consequence here is that the platform applies each; a caller cannot decline them extends to the failure return type, so there is no request field, no configuration key and no legacy mode that returns prose instead. Proposed consequence: declining is therefore inexpressible rather than merely forbidden - the typed object is the only failure return type declared on every seam and capability shape, so a component that wanted to hand back a sentence has nowhere in the contract to put it, and a failure that cannot be typed is returned as the registered adapter-unavailable type with the untyped payload in detail and counted.
invariants.quote: The platform applies each; a caller cannot decline them.

invariants.text: Retryability is read from the declared member, never inferred from a status code and never from the words: only transient errors should be retried; others require different handling, and a heuristic that keys on a substring cannot tell a transient failure from a refusal that will never clear.
invariants.quote: Only transient errors should be retried; others require different handling.

invariants.text: The dispatch seam is where the guarantee is specified rather than assumed: the seam must specify what a failure returns, so a second execution path added later inherits the type registry instead of choosing its own.
invariants.quote: what a failure returns

invariants.text: The check lives inside the enforcement path or it is not this guarantee. What runs today already has the other arrangement recorded against it, conformance checks exist; not wired into the enforcement path, and a string-match audit that only reports is the same arrangement under a new name.
invariants.quote: Conformance checks exist; not wired into the enforcement path

invariants.text: The starting state is red and that is correct. cap-errors states that this capability is adopted rather than migrated because what runs today records Typed errors | Absent (F-a6-06); the consequence for this layer is that the first audit run reports every failure site as untyped, and a green first run means the audit found no failures rather than no untyped ones.
invariants.quote: Typed errors | Absent

invariants.text: Proposed: this guarantee owns no state type of its own. cap-errors owns the problem object's shape and the closed type registry (F-b4-07); what this layer adds is only the placement rule that every boundary produces one, never a string match, so there is no persisted record here beyond the failure body cap-errors already defines, and a blueprint search for a state row owned by xc-typed-errors correctly finds none. Research query: has a blueprint search actually been re-run to confirm no state row is owned by this skill, or is 'correctly finds none' asserted without re-running the search?
invariants.quote: Typed and machine-readable. Never parsed from prose

not_exposed.text: Proposed: the detail member is not a branch key and is never part of the contract a caller may depend on. Its wording may change in any release; the type member and the declared extension members may not, which is what makes a caller that reads prose the party at fault rather than the party inconvenienced. Research query: does RFC 9457 itself state that the detail member's wording is unstable across releases while type stays fixed, or is that this row's own reading of the standard's extension-member design?

Consequence of design rule 6, which agentic-stack states under F-b1-07: the criterion a result is judged against never appears in a problem body, in detail, in an extension member or in a cause. The failure path is the path most tempted to explain why something did not pass, and it is the path a graded agent is most likely to read.
not_exposed.quote: The grader is never visible to the graded.

not_exposed.text: Proposed: no per-deployment, per-environment or per-fast-path switch turns the typing off, and no allow-list exempts a site from the string-match audit. A tolerated site is a permanent hole with a comment on it, and the count is the only thing separating this guarantee from a convention. Research query: is there a fetched source naming a per-deployment or per-fast-path typing switch as a specific anti-pattern to close, or is that this row's own extension of design rule 7's general non-optionality?

instructions.action: Take the failure object, its members and the closed type registry from cap-errors and add no shape here. This layer decides only three things: which sites must produce that object, where the count is taken, and what a non-zero count means.
instructions.why: cap-errors states that the recorded instruction for this capability is to adopt the RFC directly (F-b3-13), so a second definition of the object in this skill would be a second thing to keep in step with the first.
instructions.quote: — adopt the RFC directly

instructions.action: Put one registry instance behind every driving adapter and pass the entry kind to the problem as a recorded field, never as an input to the type decision. Assert that one refusal condition raised under each of TARGET T1's three ways in returns one identical type value.
instructions.why: Each way in is a driving adapter into one core, and adapters that initiate actions into the application core will each grow their own error vocabulary unless one registry is the only place a type can come from. The worked instances in the shapes above are the fixtures for that assertion.
instructions.quote: such as user interfaces, HTTP/gRPC requests, CLI commands, or test scripts

instructions.action: Give consumers a branch on the type member and give them no access to a message as a branch key: the caller reads type, then the extension members that type's registry row declares, and nothing else is contractual.
instructions.why: A deterministic error response contract ensures every failure can be programmatically identified without string parsing. A contract that leaves a readable message in reach will be read, because reading it is cheaper than adding a registry row.
instructions.quote: every failure can be programmatically identified without string parsing

instructions.action: Convert failure-producing sites one boundary at a time and count the remainder as untyped at each step. Never record a boundary that still returns prose as a known gap: it is the number the guarantee is defined against.
instructions.why: Proposed. cap-errors states that an untyped failure is a conformance failure of the adapter that raised it; the consequence for this layer is that the exemption is where the guarantee dies, because an adapter answering with something rather than nothing is invisible to every check except this count. Research query: is there a fetched source recommending against a 'known gap' exemption list for untyped failures specifically, or is that this row's own extension of cap-errors' adapter-conformance rule?

instructions.action: Gate the tree with the string-match audit: assert zero occurrences of failure information being extracted by matching a string anywhere outside the one path that holds the problem-details parser, and name that path in the report rather than in a comment.
instructions.why: Proposed. Parsing prose into a type is exactly one component's job. Naming the exempt path in the machine-readable report is what stops the exemption spreading, because a second path added to the exclusion list is then a visible change to the report rather than an edit to a build script. Research query: is there a fetched source recommending a machine-readable report (versus a code comment) as the place to name an audit's excluded path, or is that this row's own mechanism choice?

instructions.action: Read retryability and any wait from the declared members, and forbid a retry policy that keys on a status code alone or on a substring of a body. Where a retry loop exists, bound it by both a maximum attempt count and a retry budget.
instructions.why: Both maximum attempt count and retry budget should be set; workflow stops when either limit is reached. Attempts alone do not bound cost and a budget alone does not bound latency, and the failure this guarantee removes, a heuristic matching on the words in a body, is usually found inside a retry loop.
instructions.quote: Both maximum attempt count and retry budget should be set; workflow stops when either limit is reached.

instructions.action: Audit the paths that answer successfully as well as the paths that answer with an error, and count a result that reports completion while carrying no usable output as a failure that was never typed.
instructions.why: The worst failures in AI systems don't look like failures—they arrive with a 200 status code. An audit scoped to error paths reports zero on exactly the arrangement this guarantee is least able to survive.
instructions.quote: The worst failures in AI systems don't look like failures

instructions.action: Judge a candidate on four questions: does every failure-producing site return the typed object; is the string-match count zero outside the named parser path; does one refusal condition return one identical type under all three ways in; and is there no field, key or mode a caller could set to get prose back instead.
instructions.why: These four are what the definition of done below mechanises, and the fourth is the one that separates a guarantee from a default, since a concern a caller can switch off is a feature.
instructions.quote: Cross-cutting guarantees are not optional.

best_practices.text: Carry machine-readable context as declared extension members rather than as words inside detail: the standard explicitly allows extension members, so the context a caller needs to act has a typed home and does not have to be recovered from a sentence.

Name the failure categories that need different handling and make each a registry row, rather than leaving the distinction implicit: failures can be classified into categories including transient, contract, authentication, approval, budget-exceeded and state-conflict, and a category that no type distinguishes is a category a caller must guess at.
best_practices.quote: Failures can be classified into categories: transient (connection issues, 429 throttling, temporary server failures), contract (invalid request format), authentication, approval, budget-exceeded, state-conflict, and ambiguous-completion.

best_practices.text: The reason to adopt one shape rather than accumulate several is stated by the standard itself: it exists to avoid the need to define new error response formats for HTTP APIs, and every locally invented failure format is one more thing that a caller learns by reading rather than by branching.
best_practices.quote: to avoid the need to define new error response formats for HTTP APIs

best_practices.text: Proposed: when the audit finds a site that reads prose, fix the site that produced the untyped failure rather than widening the parser's tolerance. Teaching the parser one more phrase converts a countable defect into a permanent behaviour that no later run will report. Research query: is there a fetched source recommending fix-the-site over widen-the-parser as a remediation policy specifically, or is that this row's own extension of the audit's own design?

Do not read a green audit as a typed system until the failure population is non-zero. agentic-stack and build-definition-of-done both state the rule that a criterion nothing can fail is not a criterion (F-part-c-04); the consequence specific to this guarantee is that the cheapest way to report zero untyped failures is to observe no failures at all.
best_practices.quote: A criterion nothing can fail is not a criterion

open_questions.question: Which list of problem types is normative for this guarantee, given that a research record on file describes a closed registry of eight types including cancelled, timeout, partial-result and schema-invalid, while the closed registry in docs/decomposition.md section 2.1.6 has ten rows and none of those four names?
open_questions.evidence: An edit to docs/decomposition.md section 2.1.6, which is the only sanctioned way to change a closed registry. The research record is search-only, its URL is not a fetched specification, and its type list matches no other record on file, so it is not evidence for a registry change.
open_questions.default: 1-3-1 applied and recorded on 2026-09-03. Options considered: (a) adopt the research record's eight types; (b) treat the decomposition registry as normative and the record as an unverified restatement; (c) merge both lists into a wider registry. Recommendation and default: (b). Option (a) would replace a design-doc registry with a search-only snippet, option (c) doubles the vocabulary this guarantee exists to keep single, and cap-errors already resolved the same collision the same way for the manifest's fold-in spellings.
open_questions.quote: The registry is closed to prevent accumulation of synonymous types across the codebase.

open_questions.question: Is a grep over the source tree a sufficient enforcement point, given it cannot see string matching inside a compiled dependency, inside a prompt an agent writes at runtime, or in a language the pattern does not cover?
open_questions.evidence: Count, over one week of real traffic, how many failures were classified correctly by type versus how many callers still changed behaviour after a body's wording changed. If the second number is non-zero while the grep reports zero, the tree check is a floor and not the enforcement point.
open_questions.default: Keep the tree check as the floor because it is cheap and it fails loudly, and pair it with the untyped counter at each boundary, which is the runtime half. Reversible by adding the counter's threshold to the same report at no interface cost.
open_questions.quote: This contract must cover both structural failures

open_questions.question: Where is the untyped-failure counter kept, and who is accountable for a non-zero value: the boundary that raised the untyped failure, or the adapter that failed to type it?
open_questions.evidence: Whether a non-zero count can be attributed to one component from the report alone. If two boundaries share a counter, the report names a number and no owner.
open_questions.default: One counter per boundary, labelled with the boundary and the adapter beneath it, and the adapter is accountable, since cap-errors states that an untyped failure is a conformance failure of the adapter that raised it. Reversible by aggregating labelled counters, which no report consumer can do in reverse.

xc-typed-errors-implement.name: xc-typed-errors-implement
xc-typed-errors-implement.description: How to build the typed-error guarantee on the stack that actually runs: why there is no incumbent to migrate from, what the first implementation is when the enforcement machinery available today is a check that sits outside the enforcement path, the second implementation that moves the check from build time over the tree to run time over live responses, the three-step migration that can each ship alone, where the budget, policy, identity, correlation and idempotency guarantees land as declared members of a failure body, and the definition of done that fails when a retry heuristic starts reading words again. Load it when converting a real failure site to the typed object, when wiring the string-match gate or the per-boundary untyped counter, when deciding which of the two checks a green run has actually exercised, when a refusal has to carry a policy rule or a budget figure, or when an audit reports zero and you need to know whether anything failed at all.

purpose.text: Turn the guarantee stated in xc-typed-errors into a build on what runs here: nothing types failures today and the only verification machinery on hand runs outside the path it checks, so this facet is an adoption over call sites plus a second implementation that proves the check is not tuned to the moment it happens to run.

shapes.name: TypedErrorsConformanceReport (proposed): the machine-readable output the definition of done asserts on, one object per implementation run; it extends the TypedErrorAudit shape xc-typed-errors owns with the fields that identify which implementation produced it

implementation.description: Which of the two produced this report. A label only; no assertion branches on it.

selected_by.description: A code edit between the two runs is the finding, not the setup.

checks_at.description: The axis the pair differs on: the whole tree before anything runs, or live responses as they leave a boundary.

audit.description: The report shape xc-typed-errors defines: parser_path, string_match_sites, failures_checked, untyped, unregistered_types, per_entry.

observed_population.description: What this implementation could actually see. A build-time run sees code paths that never execute; a run-time run sees only what did.

evidence_record_ref.description: The evidence record this run was written into: script digest, commit, tree hash under test, dirty flag, and the claimed-or-measured label.

invariants.text: xc-typed-errors owns the guarantee, its scope over every failure-producing site, the one shared registry behind every driving adapter, and the audit report shape (F-b4-07). Nothing here restates it. This facet owns three things only: when the check executes, how the two implementations are selected, and how a run is recorded.
invariants.quote: Typed and machine-readable

invariants.text: There is no incumbent to migrate from. The recorded adapter for this capability is absent, so the migration is over call sites rather than over an implementation, and no measured behaviour is inherited from anything running today.
invariants.quote: RFC 9457 problem details | *absent*

invariants.text: The failure this build has to avoid is already on file in the same inventory that records typed errors as missing: conformance checks exist; not wired into the enforcement path. xc-typed-errors states that a check outside the enforcement path is not this guarantee; the consequence for the build is that a string-match audit which runs and reports without blocking reproduces that arrangement exactly, under a new name.
invariants.quote: Conformance checks exist; not wired into the enforcement path

invariants.text: The two implementations differ in when the check executes and therefore in what it can see, not in which product supplies it. build-adapter-pair owns the rule and the axis test (F-b1-04); what this facet adds is that swappability is a tested property, not an intention has a specific meaning here, namely that a build-time tree scan and a run-time response interceptor must report the same counts over the same conversion state.
invariants.quote: Swappability is a tested property, not an intention.

invariants.text: Neither implementation may invent a type it was not given. xc-typed-errors states the placement rule: 'Never parsed from prose' (F-b4-07); an interceptor that guesses a type from the words in a body is exactly the string matching that rule bans, relocated into the enforcement layer, where it is harder to see and impossible for the tree scan to find.
invariants.quote: Never parsed from prose

invariants.text: Every audit run is written into an evidence record before its numbers are read, and a run from a dirty tree is never labelled measured. build-evidence-record owns the record's fields and agentic-stack owns the labelling rule; the consequence here is that untyped and string_match_sites are exactly the kind of number that gets repeated later, and an unlabelled zero becomes a measurement the moment someone quotes it.
invariants.quote: Each record names the script SHA-256, git commit, tree hash under test, and whether the tree was dirty

not_exposed.text: No configuration key, environment flag or fast-path exemption disables the audit or the counters for a deployment. xc-typed-errors states why a caller cannot decline the guarantee - 'Cross-cutting guarantees are not optional.' (F-b1-08); the consequence for the build is that the off switch must not exist in the configuration surface either, or a zero becomes a statement about how one environment was set up.

Proposed: the untyped payload an adapter-unavailable problem carries in detail is not a branch key and is scrubbed of hostnames, credentials and adapter identities before it is carried. It exists so a human can find the site that failed to type, not so a caller can resume parsing prose from a new place.

instructions.action: Start by narrowing the return type, not by converting sites: make the typed object the only failure return declared on the dispatch seam's result shape, before a single failure site is rewritten.
instructions.why: The seam is where the contract has to say what a failure returns, and narrowing the type first turns every unconverted site into a compile-or-validation error that names itself, instead of a search someone has to remember to run.
instructions.quote: It must specify: the request shape, the result shape, cancellation semantics, timeout and budget enforcement, partial-result handling, and what a failure returns.

instructions.action: Migrate in three steps that can each ship alone: first add the object and the shared registry and convert the seam; second run the tree audit and the per-boundary untyped counters read-only and record the counts as claimed; third turn both into gates. Do not merge steps two and three.
instructions.why: Proposed. A gate switched on over a population nobody has counted turns a migration into an outage on its first run, and the read-only pass is also the only way to learn which failure sites exist rather than which ones were remembered.

instructions.action: Convert boundaries in the order of the enforcement table in xc-typed-errors' references: the policy refusal, the budget termination and the envelope validation failure first, and assert their type agreement across the three ways in before converting anything else.
instructions.why: Proposed. Those three are the refusals the fold-in requires to carry the same machine-readable type whichever way the caller entered, so they are the ones whose disagreement would be designed in if they were converted last, each by whoever owned that path.

instructions.action: Add the second implementation as an interceptor in each boundary's response path, counting and refusing untyped bodies as they leave, and change no failure site to get it.
instructions.why: This is composability doing the work the target asks of it: enhancing particular aspects of any element without touching the rest. Enforcement moves to run time, no producer is edited, and the check now runs where a compiled dependency's untyped failure is visible, which the tree scan can never read.
instructions.quote: Composability allows enhancing particular aspects of any element without touching the rest.

instructions.action: Wire the cross-cutting guarantees onto the failure body as declared extension members, adding them to the problem shape rather than to a logging helper: the correlation identifiers, the actor and its delegation chain, the spend at the moment a budget terminated a unit, the policy rule identifier on a refusal, and the idempotency key the attempt was made under.
instructions.why: Proposed. Every action already names an actor including delegated agent actors, and the failure body is often the only artifact that crosses the boundary and survives the process, so a guarantee that lives only in a log line is absent from the one record the caller actually holds.

instructions.action: Convert the consumers before the producers where you have a choice: rewrite each retry loop and each error-handling branch to key on the type member first, then narrow the producer that feeds it.
instructions.why: Proposed. A producer converted under a consumer that still matches on words changes behaviour silently, because the words moved and the match stopped firing; a consumer converted first fails loudly on the type it has not been given yet.

instructions.action: Write every audit run into an evidence record before reading its numbers: the script digest, the commit, the tree hash under test, whether the tree was dirty, and the claimed-or-measured label. Record the observed population alongside each count.
instructions.why: build-evidence-record owns the record's fields and agentic-stack owns the labelling rule (F-part-c-08); what this step adds is the population, because a build-time run and a run-time run over the same tree legitimately see different denominators, and two zeros with no denominators cannot be compared.
instructions.quote: Distinguish **claimed** from **measured** throughout

instructions.action: Run the identical audit against both implementations with the choice made in configuration only, and treat any code edit needed between the two runs as the finding rather than as setup.
instructions.why: build-adapter-pair states the discipline and the axis test; the failure mode specific to this guarantee is a check written as a grep invocation, which cannot run at all against an interceptor that has no source tree to read, so the report shape rather than the command has to be what the assertions are written against.
instructions.quote: chosen to prove the interface is not shaped around its current implementation

best_practices.text: Do not read the first green run as a typed system. agentic-stack, build-definition-of-done and build-evidence-record all build on the finding that a gate can be structurally green because the work contained nothing the tools apply to, and those establish well-formedness, not correctness; the version of it here is an audit over a tree where nothing has been converted, which reports zero string matches and zero untyped failures, both true and both meaningless.

Verify that the interceptor actually saw the response rather than that it was configured to. agentic-stack states the finding that configuration written in the documented place can be silently overridden and build-evidence-record and build-adapter-pair both build on it (F-a7-04); the version here is an interceptor registered in the right file and bypassed by one boundary that writes its response directly, which is invisible unless the report counts what it observed.

Proposed: count non-conformant bodies in the interceptor and never drop them. A stage that silently discards what it cannot verify produces a clean report from a broken system, which is the same shape of green that this platform has already measured once.

Proposed: when the two implementations disagree, believe the one that saw more. A build-time scan finding a string-matching site the interceptor never reported means that path did not execute, not that the site is acceptable; an interceptor counting an untyped body the scan never flagged means the failure came from beneath the source tree, which is why the pair exists.

adapters.maps_to: Nothing types failures today: the recorded adapter for this capability is absent, so the first implementation of this guarantee is a build-time audit over the source tree, run as one more automated verification stage beside the deployment phases that already exist, plus the in-process typing layer it checks. Its execution model is a whole-tree static scan that runs before anything executes and needs no traffic and no running system.
adapters.cannot: Cannot see a string match inside a compiled or vendored dependency, inside a prompt written at run time, or in a language its pattern does not cover; and cannot see an untyped failure at all, because it reads code rather than responses. It also cannot block anything by itself, which is precisely the arrangement PASS.md A6 already records against this platform, so it must be wired into the path rather than reported beside it.
adapters.swap_procedure: Select the implementation by configuration only, run the same assertions against the report shape rather than against the command, and require the merged report to show two implementations and selected_by configuration. xc-typed-errors owns the guarantee and cap-errors owns the failure object; what this row adds is that the audit's assertions are written against TypedErrorsConformanceReport so a scan and an interceptor can both satisfy them.
adapters.quote: Conformance checks exist; not wired into the enforcement path

adapters.maps_to: Proposed implementation, and a proposed entity id: no swap-candidate entity exists for this capability because, as cap-errors and xc-typed-errors both state, the recorded swap-candidate column is the instruction to adopt the RFC directly. It is an interceptor sitting in each boundary's response path at run time, which validates every outgoing failure body against the problem shape, increments that boundary's untyped counter when it does not conform, and refuses to pass the body on.
adapters.cannot: Cannot see a code path that did not execute, so a dormant string-matching retry heuristic is invisible to it until the day it fires; cannot read source at all; and must never infer a type from the words in a body it was handed, which would move the banned string matching into the enforcement layer. It needs a process on the response path where the first implementation needs none. The axis is when the check runs and what it can therefore see - the whole tree before execution against live responses during it - which is a different execution model rather than a different product of the same shape, and it is the axis that matters because each of the two is blind to exactly what the other sees.
adapters.swap_procedure: Select by configuration only, with no code edit between runs, and require both reports to validate against TypedErrorsConformanceReport and to carry distinct checks_at values with identical audit assertions. build-adapter-pair owns the rule that the second exists to prove the first is not load-bearing (F-b1-04); what this row adds is the observed_population the run-time implementation must publish, without which its zero cannot be compared with the scan's.

open_questions.question: When both implementations are deployed, which one enforces: the build-time scan, the run-time interceptor, or both?
open_questions.evidence: Run both read-only for one week over the same traffic and the same tree, and compare what each saw. If the interceptor counts untyped bodies the scan never flagged, enforcement belongs where the wider view is; if the counts agree, the cheaper one wins and the other stays a reporter.
open_questions.default: Both enforce, on different failures: the scan blocks a merge that introduces a string-matching site, the interceptor blocks an untyped body from leaving. Neither is allowed to invent a type. build-adapter-pair owns the two-adapter rule this question sits inside (F-b1-04); what is open is only which of the two enforces. Reversible by demoting one to reporting, which costs one configuration change and no producer change.
open_questions.quote: Every interface ships with at least two adapters

open_questions.question: Can this definition of done be run at all before any failure site is converted, given `failures_checked > 0` and `observed_population > 0` cannot be satisfied by a system that returns no typed failures?
open_questions.evidence: Whether any code path returns a problem object yet. The recorded state is that typed errors are absent, so today the answer is no for the typed half and yes for the string-match half.
open_questions.default: Run it and let it stay red, labelled claimed, rather than dropping the assertions that cannot yet pass. xc-typed-errors states that the starting state is red and correct (F-a6-06); dropping the population assertion is how a guarantee turns into a claim about the half that was easy.
open_questions.quote: A criterion nothing can fail is not a criterion

open_questions.question: Does the interceptor sit inside each boundary's own process or in a separate process on the response path, given that the first arrangement shares the failure mode it is meant to catch and the second cannot see an in-process call that never becomes a response?
open_questions.evidence: Count, over the boundaries that exist, how many return a failure without producing a response another process could observe. If that count is large, an out-of-process interceptor is enforcing over a minority of the failures.
open_questions.default: In-process per boundary, because xc-typed-errors binds the guarantee to every failure-producing site rather than to every response (F-b4-07), and the axis the pair is chosen on is already build time against run time rather than in-process against out-of-process. Reversible by moving the same validator behind a proxy at the cost of the failures it would stop seeing.

open_questions.question: The second implementation has no swap-candidate entity in the knowledge base: E-swap-candidate-runtime-boundary-interceptor is an id minted in the adapters table here because the schema requires one and the recorded swap-candidate column for Errors is an instruction rather than a candidate list. Should it become a real entity, and what does the row cite until it is?
open_questions.evidence: 1-3-1 applied on 2026-09-03 (ceremony 9, finding C9-001), the protocol the wave-4c siblings used for the same gap. Options: (a) add the id to the knowledge base, which needs a rebuild and would invalidate the provenance heads of every skill already written; (b) collapse both rows onto E-adapter-errors-absent, the only entity this capability has, which would leave the two implementations indistinguishable in the very table the swap run reads; (c) keep the minted id, say in the row itself that both the implementation and the id are proposed, and record the gap here so a reader can tell it from a knowledge-base-backed id without grepping. Recommendation followed: (c), which is also what cap-errors-implement records for the same capability row. xc-typed-errors owns the reading of F-b3-13 that this guarantee builds on; what this row adds is which id the second implementation is recorded against until the entity exists. The question closes when a ceremony rebuilds the knowledge base and the entity exists.
open_questions.default: Keep the proposed id and the row's claimed status; do not list it under entities, where an invented id would silently satisfy the validator's unknown-id check; rely instead on the adapter-entity resolution warning ceremony 9 added to tools/validate_skills.py to keep it visible to every later reader.
